To wilt means to lose firmness and droop downward because of lost vitality or strength. Think of a freshly cut flower standing tall in a vase — after a day without water, its stem bends, its petals hang down, and it looks limp and defeated. That process is wilting.

The word captures something that was strong and upright becoming weak and sagging, usually under some kind of stress.
The two main ways it is used

1. Literal — for plants (and food)

This is the original, most visual meaning. A plant wilts when it doesn't get enough water, or when it faces too much heat. Its leaves and stem lose their stiffness and droop.

"The sunflowers wilted after three days without rain."
"The lettuce wilted in the fridge because I forgot to seal the bag."
"Her potted plant was wilting on the windowsill."

You'll also hear this in cooking. When you put spinach or kale in a hot pan, it quickly loses its volume and becomes soft and limp. Cooks call this "wilting" the greens.

"Wilt the spinach in a pan with a little olive oil."
"Toss in the greens and let them wilt for two minutes."

2. Figurative — for people, morale, and effort

Here, "wilt" is used the same way but applied to a person's energy, confidence, spirit, or determination. When someone wilts, they visibly lose their strength — mentally or emotionally — usually because of pressure, criticism, exhaustion, fear, or intimidation.

"He wilted under her intense questioning." — He couldn't hold his ground; his confidence collapsed.
"The team wilted in the final minutes of the match." — They lost energy and fell apart when it mattered most.
"She started confidently, but wilted when she saw the size of the crowd."
"His enthusiasm wilted after months of rejection."

Notice the pattern: something external is applying pressure (harsh questioning, a crowd, failure, heat), and the person or thing on the receiving end gives way under it.

Wilt can work in two ways in a sentence:

Without an object (the subject wilts on its own):

"The roses wilted."
"She wilted in the afternoon heat."

With an object (something causes the wilting):

"The drought wilted the crops."
"The criticism wilted his confidence."

All its forms:

  • The flowers wilt every afternoon. (present)
  • The flowers wilted overnight. (past)
  • The flowers are wilting in the heat. (ongoing right now)
  • The flowers have wilted. (completed)
What makes "wilt" different from similar words

Wither — also means to lose vitality, but it suggests more permanent, severe damage. A withered plant is shrunken and dying, possibly beyond recovery. A wilted plant just needs water. So "wilt" is often temporary; "wither" is more final.

"The flowers wilted" → they might recover with water.
"The flowers withered" → they are likely dead or drying up.

Droop — focuses purely on the physical downward sag. It describes the position, not the process of losing vitality.

"The branch drooped under the weight of snow." (drooping due to weight, not loss of water)
"The flowers wilted." (losing inner strength and then drooping)

Flag — used figuratively (like wilt), but specifically for energy or enthusiasm slowing down, not collapsing. "His energy flagged" means it faded gradually. "He wilted" means he gave out more suddenly or completely.

"Wilt" has a slightly defeated, helpless quality to it. When a person wilts, they don't fight back — they surrender to whatever is overwhelming them. It often carries a hint of sympathy from the writer or speaker, because wilting usually happens when someone faces something too powerful for them.

"Even the strongest players wilted before him."

This line makes you feel the opponent's power, and also the difficulty of what those players faced.

SituationWhat "wilt" means

For a plant, to wilt is to go limp and droop from lack of water or too much heat. For a person, to wilt is to lose confidence, energy, or composure under pressure or stress. In cooking, to wilt greens is to heat them briefly until they soften and shrink. In all cases, something that was once firm, strong, or upright becomes weak and bent — temporarily overcome by a force stronger than itself.
